description: Evergreen content bank for Molly — Trevo Advisors social media. Used as fallback when live research is unavailable. Rewritten 2026-07-27 against molly/CLAUDE.md's brand-voice spec (see quarantine/README.md for what this replaced and why). Deliberately avoids hard statistics — qualitative claims only — because this content runs unattended without per-post fact-checking; a sourced-stat post added later must be verified at add-time per CLAUDE.md's sourcing rule, not copied from here.

posts.hook: 5 things that make a contractor website look abandoned
posts.body:
Slide 1: 5 things that make a contractor website look abandoned
Slide 2: No phone number above the fold. If someone has to hunt for it, they call the next name instead.
Slide 3: A contact form and nothing else. No phone, no way to just call — a website's whole job is to make it easy.
Slide 4: Stock photos of a crew that clearly isn't the crew. It reads as fake before anyone reads a word of copy.
Slide 5: No reviews visible anywhere. If the trust is there, the site should show it, not hide it.
Slide 6: A site that hasn't changed in years. It signals the business might not be either. We build sites that don't do any of this.

posts.hook: How homeowners actually choose who to call
posts.body:
Slide 1: How homeowners actually choose who to call
Slide 2: They search first. Not from a truck sticker, not from a flyer — from their phone, when the problem happens.
Slide 3: They look for a website before they look for a phone number. No site reads as no business.
Slide 4: They check reviews next. A site with reviews built in does that work automatically.
Slide 5: Only after that do they call — and usually just the first name that looked legitimate, not the best one.
Slide 6: Being good at the trade was never the filter. Being findable was. We build the site that gets found.

posts.hook: What happens when there's nothing to find
posts.body:
Slide 1: What happens when there's nothing to find
Slide 2: A homeowner needs a plumber, electrician, or handyman today, not next week.
Slide 3: They search. Three names come up. If you're not one of them, this job was never yours to lose — it just never reached you.
Slide 4: You never see the search. You never know the job existed. There's no missed call to notice, no lead to follow up on.
Slide 5: The work you're best at doesn't matter if it never gets seen. That's the whole problem a website solves.
Slide 6: We build the site that shows up. — Trevo

posts.hook: What a good contractor website actually does
posts.body:
Slide 1: What a good contractor website actually does
Slide 2: Gets a call started immediately. Tap-to-call above the fold, not buried at the bottom.
Slide 3: Shows real trust signals. License and insurance status, visible without digging.
Slide 4: Surfaces your reviews automatically. Nobody should have to leave your site to see if you're any good.
Slide 5: Loads clean on a phone. Most of this traffic is a phone, standing in a driveway, deciding fast.
Slide 6: None of this is complicated. It's just usually missing. We build it in from the start.

posts.hook: Before the website, get this part right
posts.body:
Slide 1: Before the website, get this part right
Slide 2: Know exactly what you do best. Every trade has a specialty inside the specialty — say what yours is.
Slide 3: Know who you're actually for. Emergency calls, planned installs, repeat maintenance — the pitch changes depending on which.
Slide 4: Know what makes a customer trust you on day one, before any history exists between you.
Slide 5: A website can't invent any of this. It can only show it clearly once you know what it is.
Slide 6: Get that part right first. The site is easy after. — Trevo

posts.hook: Your next customer already searched for you today.
posts.body:
Your next customer already searched for you today.

They had a job that needed doing. They picked up their phone and searched for someone in your trade.

A few names came up. If yours wasn't one of them, you didn't lose that job — you never knew it existed.

No missed call. No message to follow up on. Just a customer who called someone else and a workday that looked completely normal.

That's the part that's easy to miss. The losses that don't announce themselves.

Save this if it sounds familiar.

— Trevo

posts.hook: Nobody picks a contractor the way they used to.
posts.body:
Nobody picks a contractor the way they used to.

Word of mouth still matters, but it isn't where the search starts anymore. It starts on a phone, usually right when the problem happens.

A homeowner searches, sees a few names, and narrows it down by whoever looks most legitimate in about ten seconds of scrolling.

That narrowing happens before anyone dials a number. It happens on whatever shows up when they search your name, or your trade, in your area.

If that's a real website with reviews and a clear way to call, you're in the running. If it's nothing, you're not.

Save this if it sounds familiar.

— Trevo

posts.hook: We reviewed a contractor site that had everything except a way to call.
posts.body:
We reviewed a contractor site that had everything except a way to call.

Nice logo. Clean colors. A whole page about the company history. Somewhere near the bottom, in small text, a contact form.

No phone number anywhere above it. No tap-to-call. Just a form, on a site that's mostly viewed on a phone, by someone standing in a driveway wanting to talk to a person.

This is a composite of a pattern we see constantly, not one specific business. The fix isn't a redesign. It's one button, moved to the top.

Link in bio to see what yours could look like.

— Trevo

posts.hook: The difference a real website makes isn't dramatic. It's just steady.
posts.body:
The difference a real website makes isn't dramatic. It's just steady.

More of the calls that used to go to whoever showed up first in a search. Fewer jobs that quietly went to someone else without you ever hearing about it.

Nothing about the work changes. You're still the same contractor, doing the same trade, at the same standard.

What changes is whether the people searching for that trade can actually find you before they find someone else.

That's the whole bet a website makes, and it's a quiet one — no dramatic before-and-after, just fewer jobs slipping past unseen.

Link in bio to see what yours could look like.

— Trevo

posts.hook: The trade doesn't get enough credit for how much judgment it takes.
posts.body:
The trade doesn't get enough credit for how much judgment it takes.

Every job is a little different. Every house has its own quirks. Knowing what you're looking at before you open a wall or a panel is its own kind of expertise, built over years, not taught in an afternoon.

That's the part marketing tends to skip past — the actual skill, in favor of generic claims that could apply to anyone.

We'd rather point at the work itself. That's the part worth being proud of.

— Trevo
